title: Judging an agent's work
objectives: Evaluate agent trajectories on planted tasks, and decide when a fixed workflow beats an agent.

screens.title: Right, but how?
screens.prose: Task T14 asks for ELRY's close on 14 March 2024. The scripted model answers at once, and the answer matches the true close.

params.title: T14
lines: user: [T14] What was ELRY's close on 2024-03-14?

screens.question: Is this evidence that the agent works?

options.text: No: it used no tool, so it is memory or luck

options.why: Right by memory says nothing about whether it would look up a close it did not know.
Without the lookup there is no evidence the process works at all.

options.text: Yes: it must have used a tool internally
options.why: The trace shows no tool call.

hints.text: Which tool did the task require, and was it called?

feedback.correct: No: the task required get_close, and the trace shows no call.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the trace for the required tool.

explain.text: A right answer without the required lookup is l5's problem again: memory, not reading. Score the process as well as the answer.

screens.title: A scorecard
screens.prose: All 20 planted tasks, run by the agent with clear error messages. A task counts as a **success** only if the answer is right and every required tool was used.
screens.question: Tap every task that is not a success.

hints.text: Two endless searches, one wrong answer and one answer from memory.

feedback.correct: T10 and T20 looped, T11 answered wrongly with no tool, and T14 answered rightly with no tool.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Tap the four rows marked 'no' under Success.

byKey.r13: T14 is marked success 'no': right answer, but no get_close.
byKey.r12: T13 worked its percentage out itself; its required tool, get_close, was used, so it succeeds.

explain.text: Four failures of four kinds: two loops stopped by the repeat check, one confident wrong answer and one right answer with no evidence behind it.

screens.title: A success rate with an error bar
screens.prose: The **success rate** is the share of tasks that succeed; with $n$ tasks, its standard error is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ (`post-train` level 4).
screens.question: What is the standard error of the agent's success rate? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the square root of $p(1-p)/n$.

byKey.var: That is the variance; take its square root.
byKey.n1: You left out the division by $n = 20$.

explain.text: Success rate 0.8 with standard error 0.0894. Twenty tasks pin the rate down only to within about 18 points either way.

screens.title: Steps compound
screens.prose: A real model makes each step right with some chance, not always. If every step of a task succeeds independently with chance 0.95, a task of $n$ steps succeeds with $0.95^n$.
screens.question: What is the chance a 10-step task succeeds? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $0.95^{10} = 0.5987$: worse than a coin toss would suggest by eye.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Raise 0.95 to the 10th power.

byKey.linear: You took 5% off per step, 50% in all. Chances multiply: 0.95 times itself 10 times.

explain.text: $0.95^5 = 0.7738$, $0.95^{10} = 0.5987$, $0.95^{20} = 0.3585$; at 0.99 a step, 20 steps give 0.8179. Long agent runs fail more often than their steps suggest.

screens.title: Five points apart
screens.prose: Two agent variants score 0.70 and 0.75 on 40 tasks each.
screens.question: What is the standard error of a success rate of 0.70 on 40 tasks? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $\sqrt{0.21/40} = 0.0725$, so a 5-point gap is under one standard error: not distinguishable.

byKey.n: You left out the division by 40.

explain.text: Each rate is uncertain by about 0.0725, so 0.70 against 0.75 is well inside the noise. Hundreds of tasks, or a paired comparison on the same tasks, are needed.

screens.title: A paired comparison
screens.prose: Run the same 20 tasks with clear errors (0.80) and with 'invalid input' (0.45). Pair them by task: the difference is 1 where only the clear-error run succeeds, and 0 where both agree.
screens.question: The mean difference is 0.35. Its standard error is 0.1094. How many standard errors from 0 is it? Give 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Divide the mean difference by its standard error.

feedback.correct: $0.35/0.1094 = 3.2$: on these tasks the messages clearly matter.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Mean over standard error.

byKey.inv: You divided the standard error by the mean.

explain.text: Pairing on the same tasks removes the difference between easy and hard tasks: 0.35 is 3.2 standard errors from 0, though the 20 tasks were planted to show it.

screens.title: Grading only the answer
screens.prose: A colleague's evaluation checks only whether each final answer matches the known answer, and reports the share.
screens.question: What does that report give for the 20 tasks? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Count the 'yes' entries under Right answer.
T14 counts, though it used no tool.

feedback.correct: 17/20 = 0.85, against a success rate of 0.80: T14's memorised answer is counted as a working agent.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count right answers only.

byKey.success: 0.80 is the success rate, which also requires the tools. The answer-only report counts T14 too.

explain.text: Answer-only grading gives 0.85. The required-tool check is what caught T14; on new questions, memory will not be there to help.

screens.title: Agent or workflow
screens.prose: What you measured: score each run for a right answer and the required tools; aggregate into a success rate with its standard error; compare variants on the same tasks. Reliability compounds, $p^n$ for $n$ steps. On these tasks the fixed workflow of l11 succeeds on 20 of 20; the agent on 16.
screens.question: When do Anthropic's guidelines favour a workflow over an agent?

options.text: When the steps are known in advance

options.why: Hard tasks with unknown steps are where an agent earns its cost.
Cost is one reason; testability and reliability are others.
Here the workflow beat the agent on every count.

hints.text: What did the workflow need to know to run?

feedback.correct: When the steps are known: a fixed chain is cheaper, easier to test and as good.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What did the workflow need?

explain.text: Start with the simplest thing that works, a workflow when the steps are known, and move to an agent only when the next step depends on what the last one found.

mutants.symptom: Divides by n - 1 in the standard error of a proportion.

mutants.source:
import math


def success_rate(scores):
    n = len(scores)
    p = sum(1 for s in scores if s['success']) / n
    return p, math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)


def compare_agents(a, b):
    d = [int(x['success']) - int(y['success']) for x, y in zip(a, b)]
    n = len(d)
    m = sum(d) / n
    sd = math.sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in d) / (n - 1))
    return m, sd
mutants.symptom: Returns the standard deviation of the differences.

byKey.test-4: Divide the standard deviation of the differences by $\sqrt n$.
byKey.test-3: Return a minus b: when B is better the mean is negative.

explain.text: The paired standard error uses the spread of the per-task differences, which is smaller than two separate error bars suggest when the tasks vary in difficulty.

screens.title: A weekly report
screens.prose: A research team wants a weekly report: pull the same 12 prices, compute their weekly changes, and search the notes for each company's latest news. Someone proposes an autonomous agent; someone else, a fixed pipeline.
screens.question: What does this level's evidence support?

options.text: A fixed pipeline, since the steps are known
An agent, because it can adapt
options.why: Nothing here needs adapting: the steps are the same every week.

options.text: An agent with a larger step cap than usual
options.why: A larger cap raises cost and risk; it does not make known steps better.

options.text: Ask the model to write the report from memory
options.why: That is T14's failure on every line.

hints.text: Are the steps known in advance?

feedback.correct: A pipeline: known steps, fixed code. A model can still write the summary paragraph at the end.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Are the steps known each week?

explain.text: The workflow solved 20 of 20 planted tasks with no model call; the agent 16. With 20-step weekly runs at 0.95 a step, an agent would finish only about 36% of weeks cleanly.

ideas: Score each run on planted tasks for a right answer and the required tools; a right answer without the tool is memory or luck, not evidence.
Report a success rate with its standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, and compare variants paired on the same tasks; 40 tasks cannot separate 5 points.
Step reliability compounds as $p^n$; when the steps are known in advance, a fixed workflow is cheaper, testable and as good.
